questions.q: If n qubits are placed in a uniform superposition (equal amplitude on all 2^n basis states) and then immediately measured, what actually happens?
options: You get a single, uniformly random n-bit string — no better than guessing, since all outcomes are equally likely
You get the correct answer to whatever problem you were solving, since all possibilities were explored at once
You get all 2^n answers simultaneously, readable at once from the measurement
The measurement fails, because uniform superpositions cannot be measured
questions.explain: Measurement collapse samples one outcome according to the Born rule's probabilities. With equal amplitudes on every basis state, every outcome is equally likely, so the result is just a uniformly random string — exactly as useful as flipping n coins. Superposition alone, with no further structure, gives zero computational advantage.

questions.q: What is the actual mechanism that gives quantum algorithms like Grover's and Shor's their speedup?
options: Interference: a sequence of operations engineered so correct-answer amplitudes reinforce and wrong-answer amplitudes cancel, before measurement
Using more qubits than a classical computer has bits, which automatically yields faster answers
Measuring the superposition multiple times in parallel to recover all amplitudes at once
Avoiding measurement collapse entirely by reading the amplitudes directly off the qubits
questions.explain: The engine behind real speedups is interference — amplitudes combining constructively on correct answers and destructively on wrong ones — carried out through a specific sequence of gates before measurement. There's no way to read amplitudes directly off a single qubit, and no shortcut that comes merely from having more qubits without the right algorithmic structure.

questions.q: Why can't an arbitrary classical algorithm be 'made quantum' just by adding superposition to get an automatic exponential speedup?
options: Because the speedup comes from a specific interference structure tailored to a problem's mathematical properties, not from superposition by itself
Because quantum computers cannot run algorithms that were originally designed for classical computers, under any circumstances
Because superposition only works for problems that have fewer than 2 possible answers
Because adding more qubits to a quantum computer always makes it slower, regardless of the algorithm
questions.explain: Each known quantum speedup (Shor's exploiting periodicity via the quantum Fourier transform, Grover's using repeated amplitude amplification against unstructured search) comes from a specific, carefully constructed interference pattern matched to that problem's structure. There is no generic 'add superposition' step that produces a speedup for an arbitrary problem — the structure has to already be there for an algorithm to exploit.

questions.q: Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup (roughly √N instead of N) for unstructured search. How does this compare to the 'tries everything at once for free' myth?
options: It's far more modest — real and useful, but nowhere near the exponential, no-extra-work speedup the myth implies
It confirms the myth exactly, since √N still means searching all N items simultaneously
It actually disproves that quantum computers have any advantage over classical computers
It is an exponential speedup, just measured using a different mathematical notation
questions.explain: √N versus N is a real, provable improvement, but it is a modest polynomial speedup, not an exponential one, and it required a specific algorithmic construction (iterated amplitude amplification) rather than simply existing because qubits were in superposition. Grover's is also provably optimal for unstructured search — no quantum algorithm can do better for that specific problem.

questions.q: What is the correct framing, according to this lesson, of what a quantum algorithm designer is actually trying to achieve?
options: Arrange gates so that, by the time measurement happens, probability mass is concentrated almost entirely on the desired answer
Maximize the number of qubits in superposition so that as many answers as possible are represented at once
Avoid measurement entirely so that the full amplitude information can be used directly as the final answer
Ensure every possible answer has exactly equal amplitude so that every measurement outcome is equally informative
questions.explain: Because only one classical sample can be extracted from measurement, and that sample is drawn according to the probabilities that existed just before measuring, the real design problem is engineering the gate sequence so the correct answer's probability (squared amplitude) dominates by the time you measure. Equal amplitudes everywhere, by contrast, is exactly the useless uniform-superposition case described earlier in this lesson.
